extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, students, and general readers interested in the aesthetics of mathematical results and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the commonly cited qualities and working vocabulary mathematicians use to judge the beauty of results and proofs (e.g., inevitability, unexpectedness, economy, depth, connection, essence, simplicity). Useful for assessing or composing proofs/results with aesthetic criteria in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity, logical compulsion — the sense that the result or proof could not reasonably be otherwise (Hardy's 'inevitability').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A beautiful argument gives the impression that the steps and conclusions are forced by logic rather than ad hoc. Anti-pattern: proofs that rely on arbitrary tricks or many unrelated intermediate cases detract from inevitability. Hardy contrasted this with dull forms such as 'enumeration of cases.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise; non-obvious connections between ideas or fields (Hardy's 'unexpectedness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results or proofs that reveal surprising links or counterintuitive facts tend to be judged beautiful. Caveat: Rota (1997) argued that unexpectedness alone is not sufficient—surprisingness can exist without beauty, so unexpected connections should also possess other virtues (depth, inevitability, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency, conciseness — achieving the result with minimal, effective argument (Hardy's 'economy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, simple proofs that avoid unnecessary steps are preferred. Economy overlaps with simplicity and brevity; avoid laborious, case-heavy, or verbose arguments. Scoring note: more economical proofs are typically rated higher on aesthetic grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, simple proofs are preferred over laborious or case-heavy ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise presentation and arguments that make the idea transparent. Anti-patterns include long computations, extensive case distinctions, or proofs that obscure the key idea behind excessive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetic quality often associated with the form of exposition; sometimes distinguished from 'beauty' itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance can refer to pleasing exposition, graceful manipulations, or stylistic neatness in arguments. It may be judged separately from deeper criteria (e.g., a proof can be elegant in presentation yet not reveal deep connections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The result or proof exhibits depth — nontrivial insight, substantive reach, or conceptual richness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth contributes to beauty when a theorem or proof penetrates beyond surface facts to reveal substantial mathematical structure. Deep results often connect to other major ideas or have significant consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection (revealing links)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealing connections between seemingly unrelated areas or concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs or results that illuminate how disparate parts of mathematics fit together are highly valued aesthetically. Explicitly showing these links (rather than mere coincidence) strengthens the beauty claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence (explanatory power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal the essence of why a theorem is true, not just that it is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most beautiful proofs explain the core reason behind a result, offering conceptual understanding. Guidance: prefer proofs that make the cause visible and reduce the theorem to its essential mechanism rather than mere verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual clarity and intuitive appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that are visually clear or give strong intuitive pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrams, geometric interpretations, or presentations that make the argument easy to visualize often increase aesthetic appreciation. Scoring note: visual/intuition-based proofs may be preferred for pedagogy and perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent proofs as a sign of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Having several independent proofs is taken as evidence of a theorem's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When different methods produce the same result, it suggests robustness and multiple facets of understanding, which is valued aesthetically. Guidance: independent proofs can highlight different aspects (combinatorial, algebraic, analytic) that enrich appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of computational heaviness / computer-only verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is often associated with proofs that avoid heavy computation or reliance on computer verification (this is contested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some mathematicians view long, computer-assisted, or brute-force computational proofs as less beautiful, though this is debated. Note the meta-criterion: computational proofs can be powerful but may lack perceived elegance or conceptual insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive/explicit realisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit, constructive realisations enhance beauty beyond mere existence proofs (Monastyrsky's point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive arguments that build or exhibit the object in question can be more aesthetically satisfying than nonconstructive existence proofs. Guidance: whenever feasible, providing explicit constructions adds to perceived beauty and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of enumeration of cases (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumeration of cases is explicitly rejected by Hardy as a dull form of argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that proceed by extensive case-by-case checking are typically viewed as inelegant; strive for unified arguments that explain why all cases fit into a single conceptual framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connected values: abstractness and purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is associated with abstractness, purity, order in addition to simplicity and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results that display a kind of conceptual purity or that abstract away irrelevant detail often score high aesthetically. Guidance: purer, more abstract formulations that expose why a result is natural are prized.
